newsitem.title: UK: Analysts say Medeva poised for strong growth.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say Medeva poised for strong growth.

text.p: Medeva Plc, which posted 1996 results above forecasts on Wednesday, is poised for significant growth, analysts said.

They said optimism about prospects for the portfolio of products acquired with the U.S. Rochester business last year and for the Hepagene Hepatitis B vaccine should overcome worries about competition to its most profitable drug, Methylphenidate.

One brokerage analyst said Medeva was starting to be taken "very seriously" after several years of suspicion, adding "it might be that when Hepagene comes through we might get a rerating" of the stock.

Analysts were pleased with the performance of the 10 Rochester products, which posted sales of $77 million in the six months after Medeva took control last July compared with $100 million in the whole of 1995.

Nomura analyst Nick Woolf said the mood of the company's meeting with analyst on Wednesday was "really quite positive, especially with the Rochester products, where they have got some quite dynamic ideas in terms of sales and marketing, so that is quite exciting".
Woolf said he may raise some of his product sales estimates for the group, but added that "Methylphenidate was probably the only less positive area".

Medeva dominates the market for the drug, which is used for behaviour control largely in the U.S, where it has a 70 percent market share. Although sales rose by 20 percent last year to 108 million stg, Woolf said this was a significant slowdown from earlier years and the group is vulnerable to erosion from new entrants to the market.

However the brokerage analyst said Medeva's work on improving the dosing of Methylphenidate and its collaboration with Chiroscience Group Plc on a purified version of the drug "should enhance its position versus the competition and in Europe", where it has met resistance.
Methylphenidate continues to account for the bulk of Medeva's profits and analysts had feared that competition could cripple an important cash cow.
But Refsum said Medeva had gains from the restructuring of the U.S. business "and benefits to come through from Rochester to see them through, and they have got some blockbusters in the pipeline".

Refsum was especially upbeat about the position in vaccines. "Vaccines are everything. SmithKline Beecham was talking about the vaccine market doubling, and Medeva have a line into that through (a collaboration with) SmithKline and Hepagene."

The company has licensed Pertactin, a key component of a new generation of whooping cough vaccines, to SmithKline Beecham, and stands to gain important royalties in what some analysts estimate could be a $1 billion market.

And last month the company said results of late stage trials of its Hepatitis B vaccine Hepagene were positive. It believes Hepagene will immunise people who do not respond to current products and could also work as a treatment for people with chronic Hepatitis.

"Pertactin will be big news and Hepagene is looking like it will be a very big drug as well," said Refsum, adding that vaccines had gone from being "a high volume, low margin business to being a high volume, high margin, high growth area".
